title: Car Sharing Business
desc: Plan a small car-sharing or ride-sharing service: legal checks, insurance, booking, safety, pricing and fairness to drivers and riders.
outcomes: Explain models: peer-to-peer, fleet and carpool.
Set up booking, ID and insurance steps.
Compute cost per hour and per km.
task: Design a small car-sharing service with legal checks, driver and rider vetting, booking flow, insurance, pricing and safety plan.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, a practice case, two peers and a mentor. Real vehicles or riders are not used.
standard: Legal and insurance checks are listed with sources; cost per km is correct; vetting and safety steps are written; fairness rules for drivers are included; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Entrepreneurs, community groups, fleet staff, employers with commute schemes.
evidence: legal checklist, booking flow, cost sheet, safety plan, launch plan
modules: Models of car and ride sharing
Understand
Sharing a car can mean lending your own, booking a fleet by the hour or sharing journeys. Each model has different legal, trust and money needs.
Peer-to-peer: owners rent their cars to others through a platform. Needs strong identity checks and clear damage rules.
Fleet sharing: one operator owns cars, members book by the hour. Needs capital, parking and maintenance.
Carpooling: people with spare seats share trips and fuel costs. Needs matching and safety rules.
Choose by density, trust and parking in your community.
A residential building with 120 flats and few parking spaces runs two shared cars booked by the hour. A village with long commutes starts with carpooling because it needs no vehicles.
Compare the three models for one community in a table and choose one with reasons.
Table has pros, cons, capital needed and risks; choice is justified.
Legal checks and insurance
Apply
Sharing can void ordinary insurance. Check before the first trip.
Ask the insurer in writing what is covered when the car is shared, who is a named driver, and what is excluded.
Check licence, registration, tax and commercial rules for charging fees.
Write terms: damage, fines, fuel or charge, cleaning, late return, accidents.
Keep copies and update yearly.
An insurer confirms cover only for registered, declared vehicles and named drivers. An undeclared sharing claim would be refused, so the service declares every car and driver.
Build a legal checklist with a source for each item.
Each item has an authority or insurer, answer and date.
Vetting drivers and identity
Apply
You are responsible for who drives your cars.
Check licence, age, driving record and ID documents.
Set minimum experience and a trial drive for new members.
Re-check licences monthly and block expired ones automatically.
Protect personal data and explain how it is used.
A monthly licence expiry report blocks three members until they upload new documents.
Write the vetting steps and a monthly routine.
Steps cover document check, trial drive, expiry and data protection.
Booking, handover and return
Apply
A clear handover prevents most disputes.
App or form: choose car, time, deposit.
Photograph the car, fuel or charge level and mileage at pickup and return.
Late and cancellation rules; support line.
Release the deposit within 48 hours of a clean return.
A 2,000 INR deposit (an estimate; check your market) is held and released after a clean return. Photos show a new scratch from the previous driver, who is charged.
Design the booking and handover flow in eight steps.
Flow has times, photos and deposit rules.
Costs, pricing and break-even
Analyse
Know the cost per hour and per kilometre before setting prices.
Fixed costs: insurance, depreciation, parking, tax. Variable costs: fuel or power, tyres, servicing.
Cost per hour = fixed cost per day / hours available; cost per km = variable cost / km.
Utilisation = hours booked / hours available; break-even depends on it.
Show members an example bill before they book.

Fixed cost 520 INR per day and variable 7 INR per km. A 4-hour, 40 km trip costs about 208 + 280 = 488 INR. At 40 per cent utilisation of 10 available hours (4 booked hours), the 520 INR fixed cost needs at least 130 INR per booked hour before any variable cost.
Build a cost sheet and price three sample trips.
Maths is correct and currency is shown.
Safety, incidents and support
Evaluate
Plan for breakdowns, accidents and misuse.
Emergency numbers in the car and the app; first-aid kit and warning triangle.
Steps: make everyone safe, call help, photograph, report, record.
Roadside help and a replacement car plan.
Incident log and monthly review.
A driver reports a flat tyre; roadside help arrives in 40 minutes and the booking is extended at no charge. The log shows three flat tyres in a month, so tyre checks are added.
Write an incident plan and run a mock breakdown.
Plan has steps, contacts and a recorded mock run.
Fairness, access and community
Evaluate
A shared service should include people with fewer options.
No discrimination in access; clear and equal vetting rules.
Offer pay-as-you-go, lower deposits or a payment plan for low-income members.
Provide accessible options such as hand controls where possible.
Publish fees and an appeals route.
A rule offers hand controls on request, with notice, and caps late fees so they cannot exceed the hourly rate.
List fairness rules and a fee cap.
Rules are clear and apply to all.
Pilot and launch plan
Create
Test small and measure.
Start with one car and 20 members for 30 days.
Measure utilisation, damage per 100 trips, member score and cost per trip.
Fix the top three problems.
Decide: grow, change model or stop.
The pilot reaches 60 per cent utilisation, one minor damage and a member score of 4.4 out of 5. The team adds a second car near a station.
Write a pilot plan with targets and a decision rule.
Targets are numbers and a stop rule is stated.

Cover wording read for exclusions and the gaps listed
Licence check, background rule and data rule for the place are written down
Rules checked with the regulator and a refusal case worked through
